subject: english-literature
title: Setting, Symbol and Structure
welcome_lead: Beyond voice — examine how place, recurring images and narrative shape combine into prose meaning.
meta_desc: Setting, symbol, structure and narrative time in prose at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You can now read setting and structure as load-bearing meaning, not background scenery.

concepts.def: The temporal and spatial world of the text; not background but active meaning-maker.
A concrete image (Gatsby's green light, the conch in Lord of the Flies) that gathers larger meaning.
The arrangement of parts — chapters, sections, framing devices, chronological vs disrupted order.
Beginning in the middle of action, common in modernist and contemporary fiction.
A story within a story (Frankenstein's three nested narrators, Heart of Darkness).
Manipulation of duration, frequency and order (Genette) — flashback, summary, scene.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Hardy's Egdon Heath is more than backdrop — it shapes character and fate in The Return of the Native.

Setting can index class (Bronte's moors), modernity (Joyce's Dublin) or moral state (Eliot's St Ogg's).
A symbol attracts meaning through repetition and context. The green light in Gatsby begins as a navigation marker and ends as the trace of unreachable desire.
Frame narratives layer perspective. In Wuthering Heights, Lockwood reports Nelly Dean's account of others' stories — three voices for an unstable centre.

Ab ovo
Ex post facto
Coup de grâce
A nested frame narrative
Single first-person narration
Omniscient choral narrator
Free verse interludes

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a theme and a symbol?
options: A theme is the title of the book.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.
A theme is an abstract idea or concern the text explores (e.g. mortality); a symbol is a concrete image that stands for something else (e.g. a skull).
Themes are just symbols repeated through the book.

mcqs.q: What is the structural framework of The Canterbury Tales?
options: A frame narrative — pilgrims travelling to Canterbury tell stories along the way, allowing Chaucer to juxtapose different voices, genres and social classes.
A theme is the title of the book.
It is a religious text used in Catholic services.
It is one continuous story told by Chaucer from beginning to end.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a metaphor and a simile?
options: Metaphors are true and similes are false.
Metaphors are short and similes are long.
A theme is the title of the book.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states one thing IS another, making an implicit comparison without those connectives.
